body:
The constitutional scheme of 1935

The Government of India Act, 1935 proposed a substantially revised constitutional structure. Its principal features included an All-India Federation, a division of legislative powers, provincial autonomy, proposed dyarchy at the Centre and a Federal Court.

It is essential to distinguish between the Act's provisions and the arrangements that actually came into force.

The proposed All-India Federation

The Act envisaged a federation consisting of British Indian provinces and Indian princely states. British Indian provinces were to form part of the federation, while the entry of princely states depended on their rulers' accession under the statutory conditions. The accession threshold required states entitled collectively to at least 52 Council of State seats and accounting for at least half the total princely-state population to accede.

The required accession of princely states did not occur. Consequently, the proposed All-India Federation never came into operation.

The Act of 1935 provided for an All-India Federation; it did not establish a functioning All-India Federation. A statement that the federation actually began working under the Act is incorrect.

Division of legislative subjects

The Act divided legislative subjects into 3 lists. The distinction indicated which level of government could make laws on particular matters.

ListLegislative authorityTypical subjects
Federal ListFederal legislatureDefence, external affairs, currency and communications
Provincial ListProvincial legislaturePublic order, police, public health and agriculture
Concurrent ListBoth federal and provincial legislaturesCriminal law, marriage and divorce, and electricity

Where a subject fell within the Concurrent List, legislation by both levels was possible. Federal law normally prevailed in a conflict; however, a provincial law reserved for and assented to by the Governor-General or the Crown could prevail in that province over an earlier federal or existing Indian law, subject to later federal legislation.

Residuary powers concern subjects not included in the specified lists. Under the 1935 Act, the Governor-General had discretionary authority to assign legislative competence over such matters. It is therefore incorrect to state that all residuary powers automatically belonged to the provinces under this Act.

Dyarchy proposed at the Centre

The Act proposed dividing federal executive subjects into reserved and transferred categories at the Centre. Under this planned arrangement, major reserved matters, including defence and external affairs, would remain under the Governor-General, while transferred matters would be administered through ministers.

However, because the federation itself did not come into operation, the proposed central dyarchy was never implemented.

This differs from the 1919 Act, under which dyarchy actually operated at the provincial level.

Federal legislature and princely states

The proposed federal framework included a bicameral federal legislature. Representatives of acceding princely states in the federal legislature were to be nominated by their rulers. Their representation was not based on universal adult voting in the princely states.

The Act thus contemplated a federation combining directly administered British Indian territories and princely states under different constitutional arrangements.

Federal Court

The Act provided for a Federal Court, which was established in 1937. Its role included deciding specified disputes concerning the distribution of legal authority and exercising the jurisdiction provided by the Act.

The Federal Court became an important institution even though the proposed federation did not commence.

Limits of the reform

The Act remained a British parliamentary statute. It did not establish a sovereign Indian Constitution. The Governor-General and provincial Governors retained significant powers, and the electorate remained restricted.

Prelims focus

  • Government of India Act: 1935.
  • Proposed federation: British Indian provinces and acceding princely states.
  • Federation's status: Never brought into operation.
  • Legislative division: Federal, Provincial and Concurrent Lists.
  • Residuary legislative authority: Assigned at the Governor-General's discretion.
  • Federal Court: Established in 1937.
  • Trap: Central dyarchy was proposed in 1935 but never implemented.

[Government of India Act, 1935, section 5 on establishment of the federation, sections 99–104 on legislative powers and Part IX on the Federal Court, original legislation consulted 22 November 2026; historical account of the Government of India Act, 1935, in the Indian National Movement materials held by the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, sections on federation, dyarchy and distribution of powers.]

pictures.alt: The 1935 Act's federation and central dyarchy never operated; provincial autonomy and the Federal Court began in 1937. Legislative subjects had separate lists.
pictures.caption: Provisions of the 1935 Act that operated and those that remained proposals.

title: Government of India Act, 1935: Proposed Federation and Division of Powers

body:
From provincial dyarchy to provincial autonomy

The Government of India Act, 1935, abolished dyarchy in the provinces and provided for provincial autonomy. The new arrangements began operating in 1937.

Under the 1919 system, provincial subjects had been divided between reserved departments controlled by the Governor and transferred departments administered by ministers. Under the 1935 system, provincial ministers could administer provincial subjects more generally as a ministry responsible to the legislature.

This reform increased the scope of Indian participation in provincial government. It did not, however, remove all British control.

How provincial government worked

Provincial legislatures were formed through elections conducted under a restricted franchise. A ministry could be formed by leaders able to command legislative support. Ministers were responsible to the provincial legislature for the administration of departments under their charge.

Nevertheless, the Governor retained discretionary powers and special responsibilities. These could limit or override normal ministerial action, including to prevent grave threats to provincial peace or safeguard minorities' legitimate interests. Provincial autonomy was therefore not identical to the authority enjoyed by governments under India's later sovereign Constitution.

Provincial elections of 1937

Elections to provincial legislatures were held in 1937 under the new arrangements. The Indian National Congress performed strongly and initially formed ministries in 7 of the 11 provinces.

The elections provided Indian political parties with experience in administering provincial governments. At the same time, elected legislatures did not represent every adult resident. Voting qualifications continued to exclude much of the population.

The Gujarat connection: Bombay Presidency

During this period, British-administered Gujarati-speaking areas were part of the Bombay Presidency, rather than a separate Gujarat province; other Gujarati-speaking territories lay in princely states. The provincial constitutional framework and the 1937 elections therefore affected these areas through the government and legislature of Bombay Presidency.

This distinction matters when interpreting historical references to provinces. A question referring to the provincial administration of Gujarat in 1937 should not be answered as though the present-day State of Gujarat already existed.

Resignation of Congress ministries in 1939

The Second World War began in September 1939. The Viceroy committed British India to the war without securing the consent sought by Indian nationalist leaders. Congress demanded a clear political commitment concerning India's freedom.

When the British government did not meet its demands, the Congress provincial ministries resigned in 1939. The resignations demonstrated that greater provincial responsibility had not removed British control over major decisions affecting India as a whole.

The significance of provincial autonomy

The 1935 Act created a more substantial form of provincial administration than the dyarchy introduced in 1919. Indian leaders could form ministries and administer a wider range of provincial affairs. Yet Governors' special powers, limited voting rights and the continued authority of the Governor-General meant that India had not achieved full responsible government.

Prelims focus

  • 1935 Act: Abolished dyarchy in the provinces.
  • Provincial autonomy: Began operating in 1937.
  • 1937 elections: Congress initially formed ministries in 7 of 11 provinces.
  • Governor: Retained discretionary powers and special responsibilities.
  • 1939: Congress ministries resigned after the outbreak of the Second World War and disagreement with British policy.
  • Gujarat connection: British-administered Gujarati-speaking areas were administered within Bombay Presidency.
  • Trap: Provincial autonomy did not mean complete independence from British authority.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 9, printed pp. 121–122, discussion of provincial autonomy, 1937 elections and Congress ministries; Government of India Act, 1935, Part III on Governors' Provinces and provincial executive authority, original legislation consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Eligible voters and election officials conduct paper-ballot polling at a modest provincial polling place in British India in 1937.
pictures.caption: Provincial elections under the constitutional arrangements introduced in 1937.

pictures.alt: Restricted voters elect the legislature, which supports and holds ministers accountable; ministers run departments while the Governor retains special powers.
pictures.caption: Provincial ministers answered to the legislature, but Governors retained special powers.

title: Provincial Autonomy under the 1935 Act: The 1937 Elections and Their Consequences

body:
Constitutional negotiations during the Second World War

The outbreak of the Second World War in 1939 intensified disagreement between the British government and Indian nationalist leaders. Britain needed India's cooperation in the war, while Indian leaders demanded a clear commitment to self-government and an effective transfer of authority.

The August Offer of 8 August 1940, announced by Viceroy Lord Linlithgow, recognised the principle that Indians should play a decisive role in framing their future constitutional arrangements. However, it did not establish an immediately responsible national government.

In March 1942, the British government sent Sir Stafford Cripps, a member of the British War Cabinet, to India with constitutional proposals intended to secure Indian political cooperation during the war.

The main Cripps proposals

Post-war Dominion status

The British government proposed that India would receive a new constitutional status after the war. The proposed Indian Union would be a Dominion, equal in status to the United Kingdom and other Dominions in its domestic and external affairs, while retaining a common constitutional allegiance to the Crown.

This was a promise concerning India's future status, not an immediate transfer of full authority in March 1942.

A constitution-making body

Once hostilities ended, a constitution-making body would be established to frame India's new Constitution. Members of the provincial lower houses elected after the war would elect representatives by proportional representation as a single electoral college, while princely states would appoint representatives.

Right of provinces not to join the proposed Union

A distinctive feature was the right of a British Indian province not to accept the new Union Constitution. Such a province could retain its existing constitutional position, with provision for separate constitutional arrangements and the possibility of joining the Union later.

This option raised serious concerns about India's territorial and political unity.

British control over defence during the war

The British government proposed to retain responsibility for India's defence during the ongoing war. Thus, the central issue of immediate executive authority remained unresolved from the perspective of the Congress.

Why the proposals failed

The Indian National Congress objected to the absence of an immediate effective transfer of national authority, the continued British control over defence and the possibility that provinces might remain outside the proposed Union.

The All-India Muslim League also did not accept the offer. It sought clearer recognition of its demand for a separate Muslim state, which the proposals did not expressly guarantee.

Consequently, the Cripps Mission failed to secure agreement. Later in August 1942, the Congress launched the Quit India Movement, demanding the end of British rule.

Cripps offered a future constitutional settlement, not immediate independence. The proposed right of provinces to remain outside the Union was also different from the later Cabinet Mission's scheme for provincial groupings within a proposed united India.

The significance of the Cripps proposals

The proposals recognised the possibility of a constitution framed by Indian representatives and a post-war political status approaching full self-government. At the same time, the provincial opt-out provision and the failure to transfer immediate authority prevented agreement.

Prelims focus

  • August Offer: 8 August 1940; associated with Lord Linlithgow.
  • Cripps Mission: March–April 1942; led by Sir Stafford Cripps.
  • Promised status: Dominion status after the war.
  • Constitution-making: A body to frame a new Constitution after hostilities ended.
  • Distinctive provision: Provinces could decline to join the proposed Union.
  • Wartime authority: British control over defence would continue.
  • Trap: The Cripps proposals did not grant immediate independence in 1942.

[Government of Maharashtra, Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, Volume 10, section Cripps Proposals, Text of Constitutional Proposals Made by Sir Stafford Cripps, reproduced in the Ministry of External Affairs digital collection, consulted 22 November 2026; National Archives, United Kingdom, historical material on the Cripps Mission; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 9, printed pp. 122–124.]

pictures.alt: Cripps proposals kept wartime defence under British control, while promising a post-war constitution, Dominion status and a provincial opt-out.
pictures.caption: The difference between immediate wartime control and the proposed post-war settlement.

title: The Cripps Mission, 1942: Post-War Dominion Status and the Provincial Opt-Out Proposal

body:
Why another negotiation was attempted

By 1945, the Cripps proposals had failed, the Quit India Movement had been suppressed and the Second World War was approaching its end. Britain faced growing pressure to reach an agreement with Indian political leaders.

The Viceroy, Lord Wavell, proposed reorganising the existing Viceroy's Executive Council to give Indian leaders a much larger role in central administration. This became known as the Wavell Plan.

Main features of the Wavell Plan

The plan envisaged an Executive Council whose members would be Indian, apart from the Viceroy and the Commander-in-Chief. It also proposed communal balance, including equal representation of Muslims and caste Hindus, alongside representation of other groups.

The Executive Council was the body assisting the Viceroy in governing British India. Reconstituting it would change the composition of the existing executive; it would not, by itself, create a sovereign Indian government or a new Constitution.

The Simla Conference

Wavell convened Indian political leaders at Simla in June 1945 to discuss the proposal. The conference continued into July but ended without agreement.

The principal obstacle concerned who could nominate Muslim members of the proposed Executive Council.

  • Muslim League position: Muhammad Ali Jinnah insisted that the League alone should nominate the Muslim members.
  • Congress position: The Congress maintained that it represented Indians across religious communities and could not accept being treated solely as a Hindu organisation.

For the Congress, accepting the League's exclusive nomination claim would contradict its claim to represent people of different communities. For the League, nomination rights were central to its demand to be recognised as the authoritative political representative of Indian Muslims.

The conference failed because the parties could not agree on the composition of the proposed Executive Council.

What changed after Simla?

The end of the Second World War and the formation of a Labour government in Britain in 1945 created conditions for further constitutional negotiations. Elections held in 1945–1946 also clarified the political strength of the Congress and the Muslim League.

The Congress emerged strongly in general constituencies, while the League secured extensive support in constituencies reserved for Muslims. These results strengthened each party's negotiating position but did not settle their disagreement about the future political structure of India.

How the Wavell Plan differed from the Cripps proposals

QuestionCripps proposals, 1942Wavell Plan, 1945
Main concernIndia's post-war constitutional futureReconstitution of the existing central executive
Principal arrangementFuture Dominion and constitution-making bodyIndian-majority Executive Council
Major obstacleImmediate power, defence and provincial opt-outNomination of Muslim council members

The 1945 negotiations therefore concerned immediate administrative representation more directly than the constitution-making arrangements later proposed by the Cabinet Mission.

Prelims focus

  • Wavell Plan: 1945; proposed reconstitution of the Viceroy's Executive Council.
  • Simla Conference: June–July 1945.
  • Proposed council: Indian members except the Viceroy and Commander-in-Chief.
  • Major dispute: Muslim League's claim to nominate all Muslim council members.
  • Result: No agreement on council composition.
  • Trap: The Wavell Plan was not the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946.

[Government of India, Publications Division, Towards Independence, section on the Simla Conference, 1945, consulted 22 November 2026; IGNOU, History of India: 1707–1950, Unit 13, section 13.2.1 on the Wavell Plan and Simla Conference; Selected Works of Jawaharlal Nehru, Second Series, contemporary material on the Simla Conference.]

pictures.alt: The Wavell Plan's proposed council stalled over the League's exclusive claim to nominate Muslim members and Congress's claim to represent multiple communities.
pictures.caption: The representation dispute that prevented agreement at Simla in 1945.

title: The Wavell Plan and Simla Conference, 1945: The Dispute over Representation
